content: Seven percent of patients discontinued linezolid prematurely due to adverse events. Based on findings from the Nix-TB study, it may be necessary to adjust the dosage of linezolid during treatment in response to adverse events. This underscores the critical importance of close monitoring, patient follow-up, and adherence to adverse drug safety monitoring (aDSM) protocols. Additional studies, such as the ZeNix study conducted by the TB Alliance, are currently underway to determine the optimal dosing and duration of linezolid for treating drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB). However, the results of these studies are not yet available for review. The BPaL regimen, which includes bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, has been studied as a standardized treatment course. Modifications to this regimen, such as early discontinuation or replacement of any of its components, may lead to suboptimal treatment outcomes. According to the pretomanid product label, if either bedaquiline or pretomanid is discontinued, the entire BPaL regimen should also be stopped. If linezolid is permanently discontinued within the first four consecutive weeks of treatment, bedaquiline and pretomanid should also be discontinued. However, if linezolid is discontinued after the initial four weeks of treatment, clinicians should continue administering bedaquiline and pretomanid, following the Nix-TB study protocol, which prescribes 39 weeks of treatment within a 12-month period. Patients who remain culture-positive or revert to culture-positive status between months four and six, and whose clinical condition suggests ongoing TB infection, may require an extended treatment duration of up to nine months. Patients receiving the BPaL regimen (or any shorter regimen for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB) should undergo baseline testing and regular clinical and laboratory monitoring throughout treatment. This includes monitoring for symptoms such as fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, liver tenderness, and hepatomegaly, as well as conducting laboratory tests for alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, complete blood count, and serum potassium, calcium, and magnesium levels. Abnormalities in these parameters should be corrected as needed. Additionally, clinicians should obtain an electrocardiogram (ECG) before initiating treatment. The baseline monitoring schedule in the Nix-TB study was more comprehensive, involving a thorough clinical assessment followed by weekly patient monitoring until week 20, and then every four to six weeks thereafter. This schedule depended on whether the patient completed six months of treatment or required an additional three months (totaling nine months). Given that the BPaL regimen is relatively new and implemented under operational research conditions, it is also essential to follow up with patients after treatment completion to monitor for potential relapse. In the Nix-TB study, post-treatment monitoring was conducted monthly for the first three months and then every three months thereafter, for a total follow-up period of 24 months. However, at the time of data analysis, only about half of the patients had been followed for this duration. Detailed schedules for baseline and follow-up monitoring, including post-treatment follow-up, should be developed for any operational research protocol involving the BPaL regimen. These schedules should include standardized measures for recording adverse events. The World Health Organization (WHO) framework for aDSM should be applied to all patients receiving multidrug-resistant TB regimens to ensure appropriate action and adequate monitoring for adverse events, as well as early detection of treatment failure. Additional evidence on adverse events will be crucial for building the evidence base on the safety of the BPaL regimen in diverse settings. Monitoring changes in linezolid dosing and duration, when necessary, will also be important for informing future evidence on the broader use of the BPaL regimen and the tolerability of linezolid within this regimen. Research priorities include evaluating the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of the BPaL regimen compared to other all-oral regimens, collecting data from regions beyond South Africa, and investigating the mechanisms and molecular markers of pretomanid resistance. Surveillance for resistance development, with attention to the impact of specific mutations, is also necessary. Comprehensive documentation of the adverse effect profile of pretomanid, particularly its hepatotoxicity and reproductive toxicity in humans, is required. While reproductive toxicities have been observed in animal studies, the potential effects of pretomanid on human fertility remain inadequately evaluated and warrant further research. Additionally, studies should explore the relative efficacy and added value of pretomanid and delamanid in multidrug regimens, as well as the optimal dose and duration of linezolid use in drug-resistant TB regimens, as investigated in the ZeNix study.
